titel: Viktor E. Frankl: Life and Work

schritte.text:
Viktor Emil Frankl was born in Vienna on March 26, 1905, and died there on September 2, 1997. He grew up in a Jewish civil servant's family in the Leopoldstadt district. Already as a secondary school student he engaged intensively with philosophy and psychology and gave lectures in the socialist youth movement.

Remarkable is his early contact with the two great Viennese schools: as a pupil he corresponded with **Sigmund Freud**, who had a contribution by the young Frankl published in the *Internationale Zeitschrift für Psychoanalyse* (International Journal of Psychoanalysis) in 1924. Shortly afterward, Frankl turned to **Alfred Adler's individual psychology**, published in its professional journal, and spoke at an individual-psychology congress in 1925. Increasingly, however, he took the view that neither the pleasure principle nor the striving for superiority adequately explains the essence of the human being. In 1927 the break came: Frankl was expelled from the Society for Individual Psychology.

These years also saw the emergence of the terms that were to shape his work. By his own account, Frankl was already using the expression **“logotherapy”** in the second half of the 1920s, and the term **“existential analysis”** from the early 1930s onward. For the purposes of this course it is important to note: logotherapy did not arise only as a response to the camp experience; its basic features had been developed beforehand. For Frankl, the camp period rather became an existential test of his theory.

schritte.titel: Youth Counseling and Medical Practice before 1938
schritte.text:
After earning his medical doctorate (1930), Frankl combined clinical work with social engagement. From 1928 onward he organized **youth counseling centers** in Vienna and other cities, which young people in psychological distress could consult free of charge. Particularly well known was an initiative around the time school report cards were issued, specifically directed at students in crisis – an early form of low-threshold suicide prevention.

In the following years Frankl completed his specialist training in neurology and psychiatry. At the “Am Steinhof” psychiatric hospital he for a time headed the pavilion for suicidal women. Here he gained extensive experience with people in the most severe crises, which strongly influenced his later teaching on dealing with despair and feelings of meaninglessness.

After the “Anschluss” (annexation) of Austria in 1938, Frankl, as a Jew, was permitted to treat only Jewish patients. From 1940 he headed the neurological department of the **Rothschild Hospital**. He had the opportunity of a visa for the USA but let it lapse so as not to leave his elderly parents behind alone. In 1941 he married Tilly Grosser.

For counseling professionals, one point of this biography is particularly instructive: Frankl's teaching is rooted not only in philosophical reflection but in many years of **practical work with people in crisis** – in counseling centers, clinics, and psychiatric departments.

schritte.frage: Which statement about Frankl's relationship to the older Viennese schools is accurate?
optionen: Frankl was a student of Freud and founded logotherapy only after his break with psychoanalysis in 1946.
Frankl had early contact with Freud, then turned to Adler's individual psychology and was expelled from its society in 1927.
Frankl rejected psychoanalysis and individual psychology from the outset and had no contact with either school.
Frankl understood logotherapy as a subfield of individual psychology and remained attached to Adler throughout his life.
schritte.erklaerung: As a pupil, Frankl corresponded with Freud, who had a contribution by him published in 1924. He then became involved in individual psychology until he was expelled in 1927 because of divergent views. Logotherapy did not arise only in 1946 – its basic features already existed before the war. Nor is it a subfield of individual psychology; it is an independent approach.

schritte.titel: Deportation and Imprisonment in the Camps, 1942–1945
schritte.text:
In September 1942 Frankl was deported together with his wife and his parents to the **Theresienstadt** ghetto. His father died there in 1943. In October 1944 Frankl was transported to **Auschwitz** and from there to subcamps of the **Dachau** concentration camp (Kaufering and Türkheim), where he was liberated in April 1945. His mother and his brother were murdered in Auschwitz; his wife Tilly perished in the Bergen-Belsen camp. Of his immediate family, only his sister survived, having emigrated to Australia in time.

Frankl had taken the manuscript of his first book with him into the camps, where it was confiscated. He later described the attempt to reconstruct the text mentally and on scraps of paper as a task that had kept him inwardly upright.

Frankl's account of the camps is **not evidence that an orientation toward meaning guarantees survival**. Frankl himself emphasized that life and death in the camp were often decided by chance and arbitrariness, and that it was precisely the best who often did not return. His observations relate rather to how people under extreme conditions were able to take an inner stand – and to the fact that a “why” can provide support without controlling external events. This distinction is central for counseling practice, so that meaning orientation is not misunderstood as a performance demand placed on those who suffer.

schritte.aussage: In his account of the camps, Frankl advanced the thesis that prisoners with a strong sense of meaning generally survived and others did not.
schritte.erklaerung: Frankl expressly emphasized that survival in the camp depended largely on chance and arbitrariness. He describes how a connection to meaning could provide inner support, but he claims no guarantee of survival. Anyone who overlooks this distinction runs the risk of implicitly holding those who suffer responsible for their fate.

schritte.text:
After returning to Vienna, Frankl became head of the **Vienna Neurological Polyclinic** in 1946, a position he held until 1971. In the same year, two books appeared that established his work:

- ***Ärztliche Seelsorge*** (1946; *The Doctor and the Soul*), the reconstructed and expanded version of the lost manuscript, in which he systematically set out the foundations of logotherapy and existential analysis.
- ***Ein Psycholog erlebt das Konzentrationslager*** (1946; A Psychologist Experiences the Concentration Camp), later known under the title ***… trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen*** (Saying Yes to Life in Spite of Everything). The English edition, later titled *Man's Search for Meaning*, became one of the most widely read psychological books of the 20th century.

In 1947 Frankl married Eleonore Schwindt, who accompanied him until his death. In 1948 he obtained his habilitation with the treatise ***Der unbewußte Gott*** (*The Unconscious God*) and taught as professor of neurology and psychiatry at the University of Vienna. Numerous visiting professorships, especially in the USA, and many honorary doctorates made logotherapy internationally known.

Other important works include ***Theorie und Therapie der Neurosen*** (Theory and Therapy of Neuroses), ***Der Mensch vor der Frage nach dem Sinn*** (Man Confronted with the Question of Meaning), and ***Das Leiden am sinnlosen Leben*** (Suffering from a Meaningless Life). Recurring themes are the critique of reductionism and pandeterminism, the doctrine of the existential vacuum, and the methods of paradoxical intention and dereflection. Frankl expressly understood logotherapy as a **supplement to**, not a replacement for, other forms of psychotherapy.

schritte.frage: Put the stations of Frankl's biography in the correct chronological order.
elemente: Publication of a contribution in Freud's journal
Expulsion from the Society for Individual Psychology
Establishment of youth counseling centers in Vienna
Head of the neurological department of the Rothschild Hospital
Publication of *Ärztliche Seelsorge* (The Doctor and the Soul)
schritte.erklaerung: The contribution appeared in the journal of psychoanalysis in 1924; the expulsion from Adler's circle followed in 1927; from 1928 Frankl established youth counseling centers. From 1940 he headed neurology at the Rothschild Hospital; in September 1942 he was deported; in 1946 *Ärztliche Seelsorge* (The Doctor and the Soul) was published.

schritte.frage: Match Frankl's works to their main thematic focus.
paare: Ärztliche Seelsorge (The Doctor and the Soul)
Systematic foundation of logotherapy and existential analysis
… trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen (Man's Search for Meaning)
Psychological account of the experiences in concentration camps
Habilitation treatise on conscience and unconscious religiousness
Theorie und Therapie der Neurosen (Theory and Therapy of Neuroses)
Clinical presentation of the theory of neuroses and of logotherapeutic methods
schritte.erklaerung: *Ärztliche Seelsorge* (The Doctor and the Soul) is the systematic foundational work. The camp account is known as *… trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen* (in English, *Man's Search for Meaning*). *Der unbewußte Gott* (The Unconscious God) develops the thesis of an unconscious spirituality and religiousness, with conscience as the key phenomenon. *Theorie und Therapie der Neurosen* is the clinically oriented textbook.

schritte.titel: Logotherapy and Existential Analysis: Two Terms
schritte.text:
In the literature, the terms **logotherapy** and **existential analysis** are sometimes used synonymously and sometimes distinguished. In Frankl's own usage they relate to each other roughly as practice and theory:

- **Existential analysis** denotes the anthropological analysis of human existence with regard to its being-responsible. It asks: What is the human being, and in what do his or her freedom and responsibility consist?
- **Logotherapy** denotes the treatment and counseling practice derived from it, which addresses the person in his or her orientation toward meaning. Frankl understood the Greek *logos* in the sense of “meaning.”

This usage must be distinguished from the **existential analysis** further developed by **Alfred Längle** and the Gesellschaft für Logotherapie und Existenzanalyse (GLE; Society for Logotherapy and Existential Analysis) as an independent psychotherapeutic method with its own structural model (the personal fundamental motivations). This further development has in part moved considerably away from Frankl. Readers of the literature should therefore always check whether “existential analysis” is meant in Frankl's sense or in the sense of Längle's further development.

In addition, Frankl's students have elaborated the teaching for various fields of practice, for instance **Elisabeth Lukas** with a presentation strongly oriented toward counseling and everyday application. This certificate program refers primarily to Frankl's foundational work and its counseling-related reception.

In Frankl's work, {{existential analysis|logotherapy|individual psychology}} relates to logotherapy as anthropological theory relates to practice. Frankl rendered the Greek word logos in the sense of {{“meaning”|“reason”|“word”}}. An independent further development of existential analysis featuring personal fundamental motivations goes back to {{Alfred Längle|Elisabeth Lukas|Alfred Adler}}.
schritte.erklaerung: In Frankl's work, existential analysis provides the image of the human being, logotherapy the practice. Logos can also mean “word” or “reason”; Frankl used it in the sense of “meaning.” The theory of fundamental motivations comes from Alfred Längle; Elisabeth Lukas stands for the counseling-oriented elaboration of Frankl's logotherapy.

schritte.text: Logotherapy is rooted in many years of clinical and counseling work with people in crisis. For Frankl, the camp experience was not the cause of its emergence but an existential test of a teaching he had already developed.

schritte.frage: Which aspects of Frankl's biography are particularly significant for your own professional field – and where do you see the danger of using his life story inappropriately as a “role model” in counseling?
schritte.hinweis: Guiding questions: How would a person in acute distress react if Frankl's camp experience were held up to them as an example? Which elements (e.g., low-threshold counseling, suicide prevention, the connection of theory and practice) are professionally relevant for you?
